source.title: Effective Long-Context Scaling of Foundation Models
source.authors: Wenhan Xiong; Jingyu Liu; Igor Molybog; He-Jia Zhang; Prajjwal Bhargava; Rui Hou; Louis Martin; Rashi Rungta; Karthik Abinav Sankararaman; Barlas Oğuz; Madian Khabsa; Han Fang; Yashar Mehdad; Sharan Narang; Kshitiz Malik; Angela Fan; Shruti Bhosale; Sergey Edunov; Mike Lewis; Sinong Wang; Hao Ma

record.file_problem: Full paper; minor extraction artifacts in some typeset symbols, but the text is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures a related scaling axis—context length—and reports language-model validation-loss fits, but does not test the claim versions’ parameter, token, or compute scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper fits validation loss against context length. Context length is not one of the variables specified by V1–V3, and the study does not test V2, V4, V5, V6, or V7 as defined. It also reports downstream task results as context length changes, but those do not measure the versions’ specified scaling variables or pretraining-loss relationship.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the Kaplan/Hoffmann power-law-plus-constant form and fits it to validation loss against evaluation context length in continually pretrained Llama 2 Long models. It never varies parameters, training tokens or compute to test V1–V3. It does not test extrapolation to larger runs (V2) or shape at fixed parameter count (V4). The fine-tuning and continual-pretraining settings are not tested as instances of the same law (V5). Benchmark tables across 7B–70B are reported without any scaling fit or predictability analysis (V6). It does not compare fitting choices (V7). The context-length fit is a related but different construct. The record's 'tests/T3' contradicts its own finding that every version is not_tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that context length is 'another important axis of scaling LLMs'. They add that larger models leverage context more effectively, as indicated by larger β. Their main conclusions are about the long-context recipe: RoPE base-frequency change, data quality over length, and continual pretraining saving about 40% of FLOPs.
record.recipe_differences: Fits loss against context length in continually pretrained Llama 2 models; it does not reproduce the original parameter, token, or compute scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted context-length exponent β varies by model size: 0.45, 0.48, 0.50, and 0.51 for the 7B, 13B, 34B, and 70B models, respectively.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation loss versus evaluation context length fits a power law plus constant for each model size. β rises with model size (0.45 to 0.51); the authors read this as larger models using context better.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In long-context LMs, held-out loss falls as a power law plus constant in context length, with an exponent that grows with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The scaling evidence is for context length rather than the parameter, token, and compute variables in the claim; the reported fits have no uncertainty estimates in the text.
record.rows_left_out: The context-length downstream-task trends in Figure 2 are not included as rows because they do not measure a version’s specified scaling variable or relationship. Other benchmark comparisons are likewise outside the tested versions.

untested.parts: No variation of parameters, training tokens or compute with held-out loss fits.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison. The curriculum ablation (Table 10) compares FLOPs at equal tokens, not the size/token split.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
Continual pretraining and instruction tuning are not analysed as obeying a power law in scale.
Benchmark scores rise from 7B to 70B (Tables 1, 3) but no predictability fit against scale or loss is made.
No comparison of fitting methods or setups for parameter/data/compute exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Relation changed from tests/T3 to uses_without_test/T4: the paper applies the borrowed power-law form to a new axis and reports its own models' performance. The fits have no uncertainty, and the fitted range covers contexts from 1 to 32k tokens.

versions.untested_parts: Does not vary parameter count, training tokens, or compute to test the stated power laws.
Does not test whether fits on small runs predict much larger runs.
Does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute.
Does not test architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.
Does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes as instances of the same power law.
Does not test downstream performance against model scale or pretraining loss.
Does not test dependence of the specified parameter-, token-, or compute-scaling exponents or compute-optimal split on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Llama 2 Long 7B
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss as a function of context length using L(c) = (αc)^β + γ.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus context length; fitted power-law parameters
rows.note: The paper describes a power-law-plus-constant fit for each model size; the coefficients are presented alongside Figure 1.
rows.check: The formula is mis-transcribed as (αc)^β. Since loss falls with context, it is presumably (α/c)^β + γ (extraction artifact). The variable is evaluation context length within one trained model, not training scale, so the row bears on no version.
